safetyNote: Listed as edible by the German Society for Mycology and Swiss VAPKO, but a picture or orange latex alone cannot establish identity. Confirm the pine association, zoned cap, shortly decurrent orange gills, pitted stem and carrot-orange latex together, then cook appropriately. The woolly milkcap Lactarius torminosus can look similar from above but has a hairy margin, white milk and a birch association; it causes gastrointestinal illness. If uncertain, do not eat the specimen and seek expert identification.

sections.title: Zoned orange cap
sections.text: The cap is orange to reddish orange, often about 5–15 cm across, with darker concentric bands. A young specimen is convex with an inrolled edge; later the centre becomes depressed and may form a shallow funnel. The surface can feel slightly sticky when wet. Bruised areas of cap and gills may slowly develop green patches, especially on older specimens. These patches do not mean that the freshly exuded milk is green.

sections.title: Gills, pits and carrot milk
sections.text: The crowded, bright orange gills run a short distance down the stem and release carrot-orange latex when cut or broken. The amount varies between specimens. The short, pale orange stem bears scattered, shallow, brighter or darker orange sunken pits called scrobicules, often particularly near its base, and becomes hollow with maturity. Flesh is pale to orange near the surface and may green where damaged. The spore deposit is pale pinkish buff to cream-yellow.

sections.title: Pines and similar milkcaps
sections.text: European Lactarius deliciosus forms ectomycorrhizae with pines and fruits mainly from late summer through autumn. L. deterrimus is usually linked to spruce and has a smoother, unpitted stem; L. salmonicolor is chiefly linked to fir. The pinker woolly milkcap L. torminosus grows with birch and produces white rather than orange latex. Host, cap margin, gill attachment, stem pits and fresh milk colour all matter; a cap viewed from above is insufficient.

sections.title: Edibility and colour timing
sections.text: The DGfM and VAPKO list this as edible, and the Vienna municipal mushroom advice identifies it as an edible pine associate. University of Lyon 1 describes its newly released carrot-orange latex as unchanging, while First Nature reports that latex or injured tissue can later turn wine-coloured; this variation should not be used alone to separate similar species. Latex colour should be checked immediately after cutting, along with the whole specimen and its tree partner. Do not consume a collection that has not been reliably identified.

traits: Orange to reddish cap, commonly 5–15 cm, with darker concentric zones and a depressed centre
Initially inrolled cap margin; cap and gills may green slowly where damaged
Carrot-orange latex on a fresh cut; amount and later colour vary
Short pale-orange stem with scattered shallow orange pits, hollowing with age; no ring or volva
European collections mycorrhizal with pines; pale pinkish-buff to cream-yellow spore deposit
